style: calm, natural hesitations, like explaining to a friend
slides: Let's look at some full rebuttal paragraphs on our running task. Face-recognition cameras in public spaces.
Four examples. Four different weakenings.
Here's our task again. Notice one detail. The cameras identify people whose image appears in the database.
Remember that detail. It'll matter in example three.
In the first three examples, our position is for the cameras, and we weaken the privacy argument. In the fourth, we switch sides.
First, their chain. The privacy argument.
Each example attacks a different place in this chain. Keep that in mind while we read.
First, the opening connector. 'On the other hand'. So I'm going to talk about the other side.
Then their argument: operating the cameras would harm privacy. And its explanation. The cameras identify people, so there's tracking without consent. And a person has the right not to be followed.
Then the reservation. 'Admittedly, there is some logic in this argument; however...' The harm is proportionate, given the enormous benefit.
So which weakening is it? 'My arguments matter more'. And then, like we said it has to be, the explanation of why.
When rights conflict, and we say one matters more, we have to explain why. And here's the explanation: an example.
Take the people who really were harmed, and ask them. They would have preferred the area to be filmed, despite the loss of privacy.
It's not clever to sit at home on the sofa and type 'privacy is harmed, privacy is harmed'.
Now, we don't use rhetorical questions, and we don't address the reader. But here, it kind of comes in through the back door.
We describe other people who were harmed, and the reader thinks about himself for a moment. If someone attacked me, I would prefer it was filmed.
Same counter-argument. A different weakening.
What type is it? The argument doesn't hold. Privacy? Come on. With smartphones, social media, and all the apps following us, there's no real privacy anymore.
And the explanation. The phone companies know where each phone is, and lots of databases already exist. So the cameras just add one more. And you didn't protest against all the others.
This is a 'does not hold' weakening that works, because it shows why. With a fact about phones. And notice the hedge: many people, not everyone.
Again, the same counter-argument.
Now this is an interesting weakening. It seems to say: this argument isn't true.
But wait. Where did the writer get that from? That only people with a criminal record are in the database?
Remember the task. The systems identify, with high certainty, people whose image appears in the database. That's given.
But who's in the database? That's not given. Maybe every citizen, from driving licences or passports. We don't know.
So separate what's given from what's assumed. Stating 'only offenders are in it' as a fact would be a weakness.
But the writer takes it one step further: 'and it can even be determined in advance'. He offers it as a solution to the privacy problem.

So it's 'not true' plus a solution. A very high level of critical thinking. And we can add the common good against the good of one person. Whose privacy is harmed? That of people with a criminal record.
Now an example from the other side. Our position is against the cameras.
The supporters' chain: cameras in public spaces, so offenders are deterred or caught there, so the public is safer.
Test the arrows. The weak one is 'offenders are deterred in public space, so the public is safer'. Deterred offenders don't necessarily stop. They might move.
And that's where the weakening will attack.
Their argument is the one from example two. In the age of smartphones, the privacy argument does not hold, so security matters more.
The reservation: 'even if this argument is accepted'. Fine, privacy isn't that important. And then: the cameras may do a disservice to the very people they're meant to protect.
A disservice. That's something you do to help someone, that ends up harming them.
And notice the hedge at the end. Not 'no one around', that's too absolute, but 'fewer people around'. A neighbour might still hear. But it's clearly easier for an offender there.
This is a really, really nice weakening. It's the reversal type.
I take the other side's strongest argument. We're here to protect your security and your property, so we put up cameras.

And I turn it over. I pull the rug out from under their feet. You want to protect our security? Actually, you might cause more harm. Offenders move to private space, where there are no cameras. But the people there are the same people.
Maybe it's not something you'll find in every task. But I really want you to look for it when you practise.
Let's sum up the four examples. The type, and where on the chain each one hit.
Mine matters more, attacking the weight. Doesn't hold, attacking the last arrow. Not true plus a solution, attacking the first. And the reversal, attacking their key arrow, in the same field.
When you practise, go through all the guiding questions. And write their chain first. It tells you where to look.
